summary: The day lends itself to two one-statement SQL tasks, fixing the column types of a CREATE TABLE and writing a rerunnable CREATE TABLE from a column list, while its Docker, RDBMS, SQL-prompt, DESCRIBE and ERD steps are tools, concepts, MySQL-only statements or diagrams read aloud.

steps.title: MySQL in a Docker container
steps.reason: The step teaches a tool: docker pull, run, exec and volumes, and the mysql client. None of it is a SQL statement, and the page has no terminal or Docker.

steps.title: Why a relational database
steps.reason: The step argues a concept (whole-file saves, one fact in one place, rules the server enforces, many writers), and its one SQL-shaped idea, strict mode refusing a value that does not fit, is behaviour SQLite does not have, so a check would fake it.

steps.title: What SQL is
steps.reason: The step teaches what kind of language SQL is, the semicolon at the mysql> prompt and a house style; those are client behaviour and conventions, and its only statements, SELECT 1 + 1 and SELECT VERSION(), have no wrong answer but not writing them (VERSION() is also MySQL-only and a function deferred to Thursday).

steps.title: Schemas and table structure
steps.reason: The step teaches vocabulary (schema, row, column, field, NULL) and statements SQLite lacks: CREATE DATABASE, USE, SHOW TABLES, DESCRIBE, SHOW CREATE TABLE and information_schema. The critic's SQL-days rule keeps DESCRIBE and SHOW at none until ix-sql lands.

steps.title: SQL data types
steps.reason: Type choice shows up in a CREATE TABLE's declared types, which SQLite keeps exactly as written and a check reads back through pragma_table_info; the page names the slips (FLOAT for money, CHAR for a short value whose length varies, TIMESTAMP for times written with no zone). SQLite does not enforce lengths, so no check can test a value being refused, only the declared type text.

steps.title: Data modelling and reading an ERD
steps.reason: The step teaches modelling on paper and reading boxes and crow's feet aloud; turning a box into a table is step 6's CREATE TABLE, so a task here would repeat t2, and its slip (reading a line backwards) is a sentence said aloud, not a statement's result.

steps.title: Defining the schema with CREATE TABLE
steps.reason: A CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS with plain types runs unchanged on SQLite 3.39 and MySQL 9.7, and its effect is checkable: the table's columns and declared types read back, and running the statement a second time raises no error. The page's slips map to checks: leaving out IF NOT EXISTS fails the rerun, a comma after the last column is refused outright, and VARCHAR(255) for every text column fails the type check. The shell redirect and DESCRIBE parts of the step stay out.

tasks.title: SQL data types
tasks.idea: A fix-it task: the starter holds a CREATE TABLE for the desk's support plans, plans (plan_code, name, monthly_fee, created_at), with the wrong type on each column (VARCHAR(255) for a code that is always three letters such as PRO, CHAR(3) for a name whose length varies, FLOAT for the fee, TIMESTAMP for a time written with no zone). The reader changes only the types, to CHAR(3), VARCHAR(50), DECIMAL(8,2) and DATETIME, as the task text describes each column.
checks: plan_code is declared CHAR(3), because every code has exactly three letters; leaving it VARCHAR(255) fails.
name is declared VARCHAR(50); keeping CHAR because names are short fails, since their length varies.
monthly_fee is declared DECIMAL(8,2); FLOAT or DOUBLE for money fails, because those types are approximate.
created_at is declared DATETIME; TIMESTAMP fails, because it shifts zoneless times through UTC and stops in 2038.
tasks.q: The starter's CREATE TABLE for the desk's support plans gives every column of plans the wrong type. Change only the types, keeping the table and column names as they are, so that each column fits what it holds: plan_code is always exactly three letters, such as PRO; name is text of up to 50 characters whose length varies, such as Basic or Business; monthly_fee is money, exact to the cent and never more than 999999.99; created_at is a date and a time written with no time zone, such as 2026-10-26 09:00:00. The checks run your statement on an empty database and read back the type declared for each column.
tasks.starter:
QUERY = """
CREATE TABLE plans (
    plan_code VARCHAR(255),
    name CHAR(3),
    monthly_fee FLOAT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP
);
"""
tasks.tests:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
conn.execute(QUERY)
types = {row[1]: row[2].upper().replace(" ", "") for row in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(plans)")}
assert types.get("plan_code") == "CHAR(3)", "plan_code has the type for a value that is always three characters long"
assert types.get("name") == "VARCHAR(50)", "name has the type for text whose length varies, up to 50 characters"
assert types.get("monthly_fee") == "DECIMAL(8,2)", "monthly_fee has an exact type that holds money up to 999999.99"
assert types.get("created_at") == "DATETIME", "created_at keeps a date and time with no time zone as written, past 2038"

tasks.title: Defining schema
tasks.idea: The reader writes one CREATE TABLE statement for a new desk table, teams, from a column list in the task text: team_id INT, name VARCHAR(50), lead_agent_id INT, in that order, with no keys or rules, so the schema file can be rerun. The model answer is CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS teams (team_id INT, name VARCHAR(50), lead_agent_id INT); written one column per line.
checks: The teams table has the columns team_id, name and lead_agent_id, in that order, with the declared types INT, VARCHAR(50) and INT; VARCHAR(255) for name fails.
Running the same statement a second time raises no error; a statement without IF NOT EXISTS fails.
No column of teams is a key; adding PRIMARY KEY to team_id because the ERD marks it fails, since today's tables carry types only.
